Which food molecule is given as the example that is broken down in respiration?
Food molecules such as glucose are broken down during respiration to release energy.
Which gas is required for the complete oxidation of food in aerobic respiration?
In aerobic respiration, oxygen is required for the complete oxidation of food molecules.
Which gas is released as a by-product of aerobic respiration?
In aerobic respiration, carbon dioxide is released as a by-product.
Oxygen is released as a by-product of which process?
Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis.
What is the ultimate source of energy for life?
The ultimate source of energy for life is sunlight.
Organisms take oxygen from the environment, which can be air or what else?
All organisms take oxygen from the environment (air or water) and release carbon dioxide into it.
Which gases are exchanged between an organism and its environment in gaseous exchange?
Gaseous exchange is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment.
By which process does gaseous exchange occur?
In diffusion, molecules move from a region of which concentration to a region of lower concentration?
Diffusion is a process in which molecules move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Breathing is which kind of process?
Breathing is the physical process in which animals move air into and out of their body.
Animals breathe to get which gas from the air?
Animals breathe to get oxygen from air and to release carbon dioxide in it.
In breathing, fresh air is made available to the respiratory surface of which organ?
In breathing, fresh air is made available to the respiratory surface of the lung for gaseous exchange.
Compared with the blood, what is the oxygen concentration of fresh air in the lungs?
Fresh air has a higher concentration of oxygen than the blood, so oxygen diffuses into the blood.
Which process is the chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells?
Cellular respiration is a chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells, whereas breathing is only the physical movement of air.
In Fig. 10.1, in which process is oxygen used to oxidise food and carbon dioxide produced?
Oxygen is used to oxidise food and carbon dioxide is produced during cellular respiration.
Respiration at the cellular level is known as:
At the cellular level, respiration is the oxidation of food molecules with the release of energy.
Which process do the green parts of a plant carry out, in addition to respiration, during the daytime?
During the daytime, all plant cells carry out respiration, while the green parts also carry out photosynthesis.
Leaves use the carbon dioxide produced during which process for photosynthesis?
For photosynthesis, leaves use the carbon dioxide produced during respiration and also take carbon dioxide from the environment.
Leaves use the oxygen produced during which process for respiration?
For respiration, leaves use the oxygen produced during photosynthesis.
Which gas do leaves take in from the environment during the daytime?
During the daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen.
Which gas do leaves release into the environment during the daytime?
During the daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen.
Which gas do plant cells take in from the environment at night?
At night, plant cells take in oxygen from the environment.
Which gas do plant cells release into the environment at night?
At night, plant cells release carbon dioxide into the environment.
Which process do all plant cells carry out at night?
At night all plant cells carry out respiration.
What is the outer surface of the root, stem and leaves called?
The outer surface of the root, stem and leaves is called the epidermis.
Through which structures does air move in and out in leaves and young stems?
In leaves and young stems, air moves in and out through the stomata.
Stomata are present in the epidermis of leaves and which other plant part?
Stomata are present in the epidermis of leaves and young stems.
What are the special pores in the bark of woody stems called?
The special pores in the bark of woody stems are called lenticels.
What covers the entire surface of woody stems?
In woody stems, the entire surface is covered by bark.
Through which structure of woody stems can gaseous exchange not occur?
Gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark.
Lenticels allow gaseous exchange in which kind of stems?
Lenticels allow gaseous exchange in woody stems.
What does a large surface area allow, for the amount of gas diffusing in and out at the same time?
A large surface area allows more gas to diffuse in and out at the same time.
Tilling helps soil drainage and which other property?
Farmers and gardeners till the soil, which helps soil drainage and aeration.
Air spaces in tilled soil allow better gas exchange between the air and which plant part?
The air spaces in tilled soil allow better exchange of gases between the roots and the air.
Which part, besides the cuticle and mesophyll, is labelled in the leaf diagram of Fig. 10.2 (b)?
In the gaseous exchange diagram of a leaf (Fig. 10.2 b), the labelled parts are the cuticle, mesophyll and stoma.
What does Fig. 10.3 show in a bark?
Fig. 10.3 shows lenticels in a bark.
In the bicarbonate indicator activity, which colour shows that the carbon dioxide level has increased?
In the bicarbonate indicator activity, the indicator turns yellow when the carbon dioxide level increases.
In the bicarbonate indicator activity, which colour shows that the carbon dioxide level has decreased?
In the bicarbonate indicator activity, the indicator turns purple when the carbon dioxide level decreases.
What is the colour of the bicarbonate indicator at the normal carbon dioxide level?
The bicarbonate indicator is red at the normal carbon dioxide level.
A leaf is kept in the dark in a tube of bicarbonate indicator. What colour does the indicator turn?
A leaf kept in the dark in a tube of bicarbonate indicator turns the indicator yellow because only respiration occurs and carbon dioxide is released.
In the bicarbonate indicator activity, what is the tube without a leaf called?
In the leaf activity, a tube without a leaf is kept as a control.
What happens to clear lime water when exhaled air is blown through it?
When exhaled air is blown through clear lime water, the lime water turns milky.
Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains which gas?
Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains carbon dioxide.
In the breathing-rate activity, what is counted for one minute?
To find the breathing rate, count the number of breaths in one minute.
What is the collective name of the connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs?
The connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs are collectively called the air passageway.
The human respiratory system consists of the air passageway and which other component?
The human respiratory system can be divided into the air passageway and the lungs.
For which mode of life is the human respiratory system well adapted?
The human respiratory system is well adapted for the terrestrial mode of life.
Which of these is the last tube listed in the air passageway after the bronchi?
The air passageway consists of the nostrils and nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.
How many external nostril openings are present on the ventral side of the head?
The external nostrils are two openings on the ventral side of the head.
On which side of the head are the external nostrils present?
The external nostrils are openings on the ventral side of the head.
The external nostrils allow outside air to enter which structures?
The external nostrils allow air from outside into the two nasal cavities.
In the nasal cavities, air is warmed, moistened and freed from what?
In the nasal cavities, air is warmed, moistened and freed from dust.
Which structures of the nasal cavity, along with the mucous membrane, free the air from dust?
In the nasal cavities, dust is removed from the air by the hairs and the mucous membrane.
Through which organ should we breathe to keep ourselves healthy?
We should breathe through the nose and not through the mouth to keep ourselves healthy.
Which muscular passage, about 4.5 inches long, receives air from the nasal cavities?
The pharynx is a muscular passage about 4.5 inches long into which the nasal cavities lead.
About how long is the pharynx?
The pharynx is about 4.5 inches long.
The tonsils and adenoids are organs of which type of tissue?
The tonsils and adenoids in the pharynx are organs of lymphatic tissue.
What do the tonsils and adenoids trap and filter?
The tonsils and adenoids trap and filter microorganisms.
In which part of the air passageway are the tonsils and adenoids found?
The tonsils and adenoids are found in the pharynx.
At the back of the pharynx, the glottis opens into which tube?
At the back of the pharynx, one passage opens into the esophagus and the other opens through the glottis into the trachea.
On which side does the passage from the back of the pharynx open into the esophagus?
At the back of the pharynx, one passage opens into the esophagus on the dorsal side.
On which side of the pharynx does the glottis lead into the trachea?
The glottis leads into the trachea on the ventral side.
What is the opening that leads from the back of the pharynx into the trachea called?
The opening through which air passes into the trachea is called the glottis.
What does the epiglottis prevent from entering the larynx?
The epiglottis prevents food from entering the larynx.
Which part of the air passageway is also called the voice box?
The voice box is the larynx.
From which part does air move into the larynx?
Air moves into the larynx from the pharynx.
The larynx surrounds the upper part of which tube?
The larynx surrounds the upper part of the trachea.
The cavity of the larynx is lined by which kind of membrane?
The cavity of the larynx is lined by a mucous membrane.
Which part of the air passageway is also called the windpipe?
The wind pipe is the trachea.
Relative to the esophagus, on which side does the trachea lie?
The trachea lies ventral to the esophagus.
The trachea extends to the chest cavity. What is the chest cavity also called?
The trachea extends to the chest cavity, which is also called the thorax.
Which feature describes the inner surface of the trachea, which also secretes mucus?
The inner surface of the trachea is ciliated and secretes mucus.
What does the inner surface of the trachea secrete to filter, moisten and warm the incoming air?
The inner surface of the trachea secretes mucus, which helps to filter, moisten and warm the incoming air.
How many C-shaped cartilaginous rings does the trachea have?
The trachea has 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings.
What is the shape of the cartilaginous rings of the trachea?
The cartilaginous rings of the trachea are C-shaped.
The cartilaginous rings keep the air passage open by preventing the trachea from:
The cartilaginous rings prevent the trachea from collapsing and keep the air passage open.
Compared with those of the trachea, how are the cartilaginous rings of the bronchi?
The cartilaginous rings of the bronchi are smaller than those of the trachea.
What are the smaller bronchi of 1 mm diameter or less called?
Smaller bronchi of 1 mm diameter or less are called bronchioles.
What is the maximum diameter of a bronchiole?
Bronchioles have a diameter of 1 mm or less.
Each bronchiole ends in a duct that opens in a cluster of:
Each bronchiole ends in a duct that opens in a cluster of alveoli.
An alveolus is a microscopic, thin-walled pouch at the end of a bronchiole.
The alveoli resemble bunches of which fruit?
The alveoli resemble bunches of grapes.
The alveoli provide the surface for which process?
The alveoli provide the surface for gaseous exchange.
The walls of the alveoli are covered with a network of which vessels?
The walls of the alveoli are covered with a network of blood capillaries.
Which feature of the alveolar wall makes the alveoli an excellent site for gaseous exchange?
The alveoli are very thin-walled, which makes them an excellent site for gaseous exchange.
Which part follows the pharynx in the path of air?
In the path of air, the pharynx is followed by the larynx.
Into which tubes does the trachea divide in the path of air?
In the path of air, the trachea divides into the bronchi.
The bronchi sub-divide and lead to which tubes?
In the path of air, the bronchi sub-divide and lead to the bronchioles.
In the path of air, the bronchioles end in clusters of:
In the path of air, the bronchioles end in clusters of alveoli.
Through which structures does air first enter the body?
The part of the air passageway through which air first enters the body is the external nostrils.
After gaseous exchange, how does air move from the lungs to the outside?
Through a different set of tubes
After gaseous exchange, air moves from the lungs to the outside through the same connected tubes.
Air passes through the larynx before reaching which tube, which divides into the bronchi?
Air passes through the larynx before reaching the trachea, which divides into the bronchi.
Which of the following is NOT a part of the air passageway?
The diaphragm is not a part of the air passageway.
Which of the following is NOT a function of the nasal cavities?
Producing the voice is not a function of the nasal cavities, which warm, moisten and free the air from dust.
From above and the sides, what encloses the lungs?
From above and the sides, the lungs are enclosed by the chest wall.
Which thick muscular structure lies below the lungs?
Below the lungs there is a thick muscular structure called the diaphragm.
What is the double membrane that encloses each lung called?
Each lung is enclosed in a double membrane called the pleura.
What is the fluid present in the pleura called?
The fluid present in the pleura is called the pleural fluid.
The pleural fluid makes which movements of the lungs easy: expansion and what?
The pleural fluid makes the movements of the lungs, i.e. expansion and contraction, easy.
The size of the lungs of an organism is related to its activities and what else?
The size of the lungs of an organism is related to its activities and body form.
What can be said about the lungs of a cheetah and an elephant?
The cheetah and the elephant have large lungs.
Which sinuses are labelled in Fig. 10.5?
The sinuses labelled in the general outline of the respiratory system (Fig. 10.5) are the ethmoid sinuses.
Which structure, along with the pleural cavity and both lungs, is labelled in Fig. 10.4?
Fig. 10.4 shows the pleural cavity, right lung, left lung and the diaphragm.
What is the taking in of air called?
The taking in of air is called inspiration.
What is the letting out of air called?
The letting out of air is called expiration.
Air moves into the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is ____ than the pressure outside the body.
Air moves into the lungs when the air pressure in the lungs is lower than the pressure outside the body.
Air moves out of the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is ____ than the atmospheric pressure.
Air moves out of the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is greater than the atmospheric pressure.
Which structure bounds the thorax on the ventral side?
The thorax is bound by the sternum on the ventral side.
Which structure bounds the thorax on the dorsal side?
The thorax is bound by the backbone on the dorsal side.
Which structure bounds the thorax at the posterior end?
The thorax is bound by the diaphragm at the posterior end.
The sternum is the chest bone.
What is the shape of the diaphragm at rest?
The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscles.
The diaphragm is a sheet of which type of muscles?
The diaphragm is a sheet of skeletal muscles.
The diaphragm separates the chest cavity from which cavity?
The diaphragm separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity.
What are the muscles in between the ribs called?
The muscles in between the ribs are called intercostal muscles.
What happens to the muscles of the diaphragm during inspiration?
During inspiration, the muscles of the diaphragm contract.
What shape does the diaphragm take during inspiration?
During inspiration, the diaphragm becomes flat instead of dome-shaped.
What happens to the intercostal muscles during inspiration?
During inspiration, the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract.
What happens to the pressure in the lungs during inspiration?
During inspiration, the pressure in the lungs decreases.
What happens to the muscles of the ribs and the diaphragm during expiration?
During expiration, the muscles of the ribs and the diaphragm relax.
What shape does the diaphragm take during expiration?
During expiration, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped.
In which direction does the ribcage move during expiration?
During expiration, the ribcage goes down to its original position.
What happens to the volume of the chest cavity during expiration?
During expiration, the volume of the chest cavity decreases.
What happens to the air in the lungs during expiration?
During expiration, air is expelled from the lungs.
In which direction does the diaphragm move during inhalation (Fig. 10.6)?
In Fig. 10.6, the diaphragm moves down during inhalation.
In which direction does the diaphragm move during exhalation (Fig. 10.6)?
In Fig. 10.6, the diaphragm moves up during exhalation.
The diaphragm is flat and the ribs move out. This occurs during:
When the diaphragm is flat and the ribs move out, the person is in the phase of inspiration.
In Fig. 10.6, what do the rib muscles do while the rib cage gets smaller?
In Fig. 10.6, the rib cage gets smaller as the rib muscles relax during exhalation.
Which of the following is NOT an event of expiration?
Pressure on the lungs decreases is not an event of expiration; there the pressure increases.
Oxygen from the alveoli diffuses into which vessels?
Oxygen from the alveoli diffuses into the blood capillaries.
How is the oxygen concentration of the blood that enters the capillaries around the alveoli?
The blood entering the capillaries around the alveoli has a low oxygen concentration.
Compared with the blood entering the capillaries, how is the oxygen concentration of the inhaled air in the alveoli?
The inhaled air present in the alveoli has a higher oxygen concentration than the blood entering the capillaries.
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood of the capillaries and into which structures?
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood and into the alveoli.
By which process do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveoli?
Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveoli by diffusion.
Through which vessel does deoxygenated blood reach the capillaries around an alveolus (Fig. 10.7)?
Deoxygenated blood reaches the capillaries around an alveolus through an arteriole.
Through which vessel does oxygenated blood return from an alveolus (Fig. 10.7)?
After gaseous exchange, oxygenated blood returns from the alveolus through a venule.
Oxygen from the lungs enters into the blood due to:
Less affinity of O₂ for air
Higher affinity of CO₂ for air
Oxygen from the lungs enters into the blood due to diffusion.
Expired air has more carbon dioxide because carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into which structures?
The air breathed out has more carbon dioxide because carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
What is the rate of breathing, in times per minute, under resting conditions?
Under resting conditions, the rate of breathing is 15–20 times per minute.
Up to how many times per minute does the breathing rate rise during exercise?
During exercise, the rate of breathing increases up to 30–40 times per minute.
What happens to the rate of breathing during exercise?
During exercise, the rate of breathing increases instantly.
During exercise, more of which gas is required for the oxidation of glucose to get more energy?
During exercise, more oxygen is required for the oxidation of glucose molecules to get more energy.
Where does the extra carbon dioxide produced during exercise accumulate?
During exercise, more carbon dioxide is produced, which accumulates in the blood.
Which part of the brain is the breathing centre?
The medulla of the brain is the breathing centre.
What does the medulla detect in increased amounts in the blood during exercise?
During exercise, the medulla detects more carbon dioxide in the blood.
To which muscles does the medulla send nerve impulses at greater speed during exercise: rib muscles and the:
During exercise, the medulla sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and rib muscles at greater speed.
What happens to the speed of contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and rib muscles during exercise?
During exercise, the speed of contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and rib muscles increases.
During exercise, both the rate and which other feature of breathing increase?
During exercise, the increased nerve impulses raise both the rate and the depth of breathing.
Why is a morning walk beneficial for gaseous exchange? It increases the rate and depth of:
Walking in the morning increases the rate and depth of breathing, so more oxygen is taken into the blood.
Compared with the breathing rate during exercise, how is the breathing rate at rest?
Compared with the breathing rate during exercise, the breathing rate at rest is lower.
What percentage of oxygen does inspired air contain?
What percentage of oxygen does expired air contain?
What percentage of carbon dioxide does inspired air contain?
What percentage of carbon dioxide does expired air contain?
How are the water vapours in expired air?
The water vapours in expired air are saturated.
How are the water vapours in inspired air?
The water vapours in inspired air are variable.
What is the temperature of expired air?
The temperature of expired air is 38 °C.
How is the temperature of inspired air?
The temperature of inspired air is variable.
Compared with inspired air, how much oxygen does expired air contain?
Compared with inspired air, expired air contains less oxygen.
Compared with inspired air, how much carbon dioxide does expired air contain?
Compared with inspired air, expired air contains more carbon dioxide.
How many times more carbon dioxide does expired air (4%) contain than inspired air (0.04%)?
The carbon dioxide in expired air (4%) is 100 times that in inspired air (0.04%).
By how much does the oxygen percentage fall from inspired air (21%) to expired air (16%)?
The oxygen percentage falls by 5% from inspired air (21%) to expired air (16%).
Tobacco smoke contains over how many different chemicals?
Tobacco smoke contains over 4,000 different chemicals.
Tobacco smoke contains more than how many known carcinogens?
Tobacco smoke contains more than 69 known carcinogens.
Smokers have a much higher risk of developing which kind of diseases?
Smokers have a much higher risk of developing life-threatening diseases.
Which substance makes up the majority of the particulate matter inhaled by a smoker?
Tar makes up the majority of the particulate matter inhaled by a smoker.
Tar stains the teeth and which other body part of smokers?
Tar stains the teeth and fingers of smokers.
Tar increases the production of which substance in the airways?
Tar increases the production of mucus in the airways.
What does tar contain many of?
What does nicotine cause in the blood vessels?
Nicotine causes constriction of the blood vessels.
Nicotine increases which property of platelets in the blood, which can cause blockage?
Nicotine increases platelet stickiness in the blood, which can cause blockage.
The blockage caused by nicotine can lead to which diseases?
The blockage caused by increased platelet stickiness can lead to coronary diseases.
Besides disturbing hormonal systems and metabolism, nicotine damages the:
Nicotine damages the muscles and disturbs the hormonal systems and metabolism.
Nicotine disturbs the hormonal systems and which other body process?
Nicotine disturbs the hormonal systems and metabolism.
Nicotine increases the heart rate and which other measure of the circulatory system?
Nicotine increases the heart rate and blood pressure.
Which gas is formed when a cigarette is lit?
Carbon monoxide is formed when a cigarette is lit.
Carbon monoxide combines with which cells and prevents oxygen transportation?
Carbon monoxide combines with red blood cells and prevents oxygen transportation.
Carbon monoxide prevents the transportation of which gas?
Carbon monoxide prevents the transportation of oxygen.

Which process removes extra water from the leaves of grasses at night?
Transpiration does not occur at night, so grasses use guttation through pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Which gas is excreted through the open stomata of plants at night?
At night there is no photosynthesis, so carbon dioxide is excreted through the open stomata.
Plants get rid of different wastes in different ways to maintain which environment?
Plants get rid of different wastes in different ways to maintain their internal environment.
Which statement correctly differentiates transpiration from guttation?
Transpiration loses water as vapours, mostly by day, while guttation loses it as drops at night
Transpiration loses water as drops at night, while guttation loses it as vapours by day
Both occur only through the lenticels
Transpiration is loss of water as vapours; guttation is loss of water as little drops through pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Which gas is retained in the leaves during the day and used for photosynthesis?
During the day, the gas retained in the leaves for photosynthesis is carbon dioxide.
During the day, carbon dioxide is retained in the leaves and used for which process?
During the day, carbon dioxide is retained in the leaves and used for photosynthesis.
Through which structures is carbon dioxide excreted at night?
At night, when there is no photosynthesis, carbon dioxide is excreted through the open stomata of the leaves.
During the day, the oxygen produced in photosynthesis is utilised in which process?
During the day, the oxygen produced during photosynthesis is utilised in cellular respiration.
Through which structures is the extra oxygen released from the leaves?
The extra oxygen produced during photosynthesis is released out through the stomata.
Plants remove extra water in two ways. One is transpiration; what is the other?
Plants remove extra water in two ways: transpiration and guttation.
In which part of their cells do plants store large amounts of water?
Plants store large amounts of water in the vacuoles of their cells.
What does water stored in vacuoles result in, providing support to the soft parts of the plant?
Water stored in vacuoles results in turgor, which provides support to the soft parts of the plant.
Which process is the loss of water from the plant surface in the form of vapours?
Transpiration is the loss of water from the plant surface in the form of vapours.
How many types of transpiration are there?
There are three types of transpiration.
At what time do plants remove their extra water by transpiration?
Plants remove their extra water by transpiration during the day.
What is transpiration through the cuticle called?
Transpiration through the cuticle is called cuticular transpiration.
What is transpiration through the lenticels called?
Transpiration through the lenticels is called lenticular transpiration.
At what time do plants such as grasses remove extra water by guttation?
Plants remove extra water by guttation at night.
Transpiration does not occur at night. Which method do some plants use then to remove extra water?
Transpiration does not occur at night, so some plants use guttation to remove extra water.
In guttation, water comes out through small pores at the tips or where else on the leaves?
In guttation, water comes out through small pores at the tips or edges of the leaves.
Which plants are mentioned as using guttation to remove extra water at night?
Plants such as grasses remove extra water at night by guttation.
In what form is water lost in guttation?
Water is lost as vapours in transpiration but as little drops in guttation.
What does the Acacia tree excrete?
In what form do some plants store wastes in their stems, leaves or roots?
Some plants store wastes in their stems, leaves or roots in the form of harmless crystals.
Some plants store wastes in their leaves. When are these wastes lost?
Some plants store wastes in their leaves, and the wastes are lost when the leaves fall.
The plant excreting mucilage is the ladyfinger.
Fig. 11.4 shows the three types of what in a tree?
Fig. 11.4 shows the three types of transpiration in a tree.
Which process is shown in Fig. 11.5 by water drops emerging from the margins of leaves?
Water drops coming out from the margins of leaves in Fig. 11.5 show guttation.
Which of the following is NOT one of the main organs of homeostasis in human beings?
The main organs of homeostasis are the skin, lungs and kidneys.
Which of the following is NOT a part of homeostasis?
Osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation are the parts of homeostasis described in the chapter.
Along with energy and water, which gas is produced in every cell during cellular respiration?
Along with energy, cellular respiration produces water and carbon dioxide in every cell.
Blood transports carbon dioxide from the cells to which organ?
Blood transports carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs.
The accumulation of carbon dioxide can make the blood and body tissues more what?
The accumulation of carbon dioxide can make the blood and other body tissues more acidic.
The lungs act as homeostatic organs by keeping the concentration of which gas down to a certain level?
The lungs act as homeostatic organs by keeping the carbon dioxide concentration down to a certain level.
Which organ removes carbon dioxide from the blood into the exhaled air?
CO₂ diffuses from the blood into the air in the alveoli and is exhaled.
The skin of human beings and other mammals has been adapted as the organ of what?
The skin of human beings and other mammals has been adapted as the organ of thermoregulation.
A thin layer of which cells beneath the epidermis does not allow heat to enter or leave the body?
A thin layer of fat cells beneath the epidermis does not allow heat to enter or leave the body.
The skin is the organ of thermoregulation in humans and which other group of animals?
The skin is the organ of thermoregulation in humans and other mammals.
In cold conditions, goose bumps are formed because the:
Muscles at the base of the hair contract
The muscles at the base of the hair contract, the hairs stand up and goose bumps form.
Which statement about the skin in warm conditions is correct?
Muscles at the base of the hair contract
Goose bumps form a blanket of warm air
Hairs stand up to trap warm air
Sweat evaporates and excess body heat escapes
In warm conditions, sweat glands produce sweat and the evaporation of sweat cools the body.
When the muscles at the base of the hair contract, what happens to the hairs?
When the muscles at the base of the hair contract, the hairs stand up.
In cold conditions, hair and goose bumps make a blanket of what?
In cold conditions, hair and goose bumps make a blanket of warm air.
In cold conditions, the muscles attached at the base of which structure contract?
In cold conditions, the muscles attached at the base of the hair contract.
The blanket of warm air formed by hair and goose bumps does not allow what to go out of the body?
The blanket of warm air formed by hair and goose bumps does not allow the body's heat to go out.
In warm conditions, sweat is produced by which structures of the skin?
In warm conditions, sweat is produced by the sweat glands.
The removal of urea in sweat makes the skin also what kind of organ?
The removal of urea in sweat makes the skin also an excretory organ.
Dogs keep their tongue hanging outside the mouth because they have what kind of number of sweat glands?
Dogs keep their tongue hanging outside the mouth because they have fewer sweat glands in their skin.
What is the normal set point of the hypothalamus in °C?
The normal set point of the hypothalamus is 37 °C.
In fever, the set point of which part of the brain is displaced above the normal point?
In fever, the set point of the hypothalamus of the brain is displaced above the normal point.
In fever, the brain sends messages to body parts to produce what?
In fever, the brain sends messages to body parts to produce heat.
Fever helps in stimulating the protective mechanisms against what?
Fever helps in stimulating the protective mechanisms against pathogens.
Which are the most important organs of homeostasis in human beings and other animals?
The kidneys are the most important organs of homeostasis in human beings and other animals.
The kidneys are part of which system?
The kidneys are part of the urinary system.
If there are more solutes in the blood, the kidneys excrete them and do what to the water in the body?
If there are more solutes in the blood, the kidneys excrete them and retain water in the body.
If there is more water in the blood, how much urine do the kidneys produce?
If there is more water in the blood, the kidneys produce more urine.
By controlling the water-solute balance of the body, the kidneys perform which function?
By controlling the water-solute balance of the body, the kidneys perform osmoregulation.
The liver breaks down the haemoglobin of which dead cells?
The liver breaks down the haemoglobin of dead red blood cells.
The products of haemoglobin breakdown in the liver are sent to which organs for removal?
The products of haemoglobin breakdown in the liver are sent to the kidneys for removal.
Ammonia is produced in the metabolism of which food molecules?
Ammonia is produced in the metabolism of proteins.
The human urinary system is also called which system?
The human urinary system is also called the excretory system.
The kidneys remove extra water, salts and nitrogenous wastes from the blood and produce what?
The kidneys remove extra water, salts and nitrogenous wastes from the blood and produce urine.
Which tube carries urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder?
A tube called the ureter carries urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder.
What does the urinary bladder do with urine?
The urinary bladder temporarily stores urine.
Which tube carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside?
The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside.
The human urinary system has a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and which tube?
The human urinary system has a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
The human urinary system has a pair of kidneys and a pair of what?
The human urinary system has a pair of kidneys and a pair of ureters.
Which of the following is NOT a part of the human urinary system?
The urinary system has kidneys, ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
Which sequence correctly shows the path of urine out of the body?
Urine goes from the kidney through the ureter to the urinary bladder and leaves through the urethra.
In Fig. 11.8, which part is labelled as the depression on the concave side of the kidney?
In Fig. 11.8, the depression on the concave side of the kidney is labelled the hilus.
How many kidneys do human beings possess?
The kidneys are present below which structure in the abdominal cavity?
The kidneys are present below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity.
The kidneys lie on the sides of which structure?
The kidneys lie on the sides of the vertebral column.
To which body wall are the kidneys attached?
The kidneys are attached to the dorsal body wall.
Which kidney is slightly lower and smaller than the other?
The right kidney is slightly lower and smaller than the left kidney.
What is the colour of a kidney?
A kidney is dark brown and bean-shaped.
A kidney is shaped like which seed?
Which side of each kidney is towards the vertebral column?
The concave side of each kidney is towards the vertebral column.
About how long is each kidney, in cm?
Each kidney is about 10 cm long.
Each kidney is about 10 cm long, ____ cm wide and 4 cm thick. What is the width?
Each kidney is about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm thick.
Each kidney is about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and ____ cm thick. What is the thickness?
Each kidney is about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm thick.
What percentage of the blood supplied to the body with each heartbeat do the kidneys receive?
Kidneys receive 20% of the blood supplied to the body with each heartbeat.
A kidney is enclosed in a tissue called what?
A kidney is enclosed in a tissue called the renal capsule.
What is the depression on the concave side of the kidney called?
The depression on the concave side of the kidney is called the hilus.
The renal vein and which tube leave the kidney at the hilus?
The renal vein and the ureter leave the kidney at the hilus.
At which point do the renal artery, renal vein and ureter meet the kidney?
The renal artery enters the kidney, and the renal vein and ureter leave it, at the hilus.
How many regions does a longitudinal section of the kidney show?
A longitudinal section of the kidney shows two regions.
What is the outer region of the kidney called?
The outer region of the kidney is the renal cortex.
What is the inner region of the kidney called?
The inner region of the kidney is the renal medulla.
What are the cone-shaped areas in the renal medulla called?
The cone-shaped areas in the renal medulla are called renal pyramids.
The tip of each renal pyramid lies in which cavity?
The tip of each renal pyramid lies in a cavity called the renal pelvis.
The renal pelvis extends to the outside of the kidney and forms which tube?
The renal pelvis extends to the outside of the kidney and forms the ureter.
What are the functional units of the kidneys called?
The functional units of the kidneys are called nephrons.
The Bowman's capsule is what shape?
The Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure around the glomerulus.
The nephron is which unit of the kidney?
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
How many nephrons are there in each kidney?
There are more than one million nephrons in each kidney.
A nephron consists of the renal corpuscle and which other part?
A nephron consists of two parts: the renal corpuscle and the renal tubule.
What is the first part of the nephron?
The first part of the nephron is the renal corpuscle.
The renal corpuscle is composed of the glomerulus and which structure?
The renal corpuscle is composed of the glomerulus and the Bowman's capsule.
What is the first part of the renal tubule called?
The first part of the renal tubule is called the proximal convoluted tubule.
What is the last part of the renal tubule called?
The last part of the renal tubule is called the distal convoluted tubule.
The Loop of Henle has the shape of which letter?
The Loop of Henle is U-shaped.
The distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons open into a single what?
The distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons open into a single collecting duct.
Which of the following is NOT a part of a nephron?
A nephron has a renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman's capsule) and a renal tubule; the ureter is outside the nephron.
Which sequence correctly shows the three parts of the renal tubule, starting from the Bowman's capsule?
Distal convoluted tubule → Loop of Henle → proximal convoluted tubule
Proximal convoluted tubule → Loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule
Loop of Henle → proximal convoluted tubule → distal convoluted tubule
Proximal convoluted tubule → distal convoluted tubule → Loop of Henle
The renal tubule has the proximal convoluted tubule first, the U-shaped Loop of Henle in the middle and the distal convoluted tubule last.
The glomerulus lies inside which cup-shaped structure?
The glomerulus lies inside the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule.
In which structure is the blood pressure very high, so that materials are filtered out of the blood?
The pressure of the blood in the glomerulus is very high, which causes pressure filtration.
What is the main role of the kidney?
The main role of the kidney is urine formation.
Into how many sub-processes can urine formation be divided?
Urine formation is divided into three sub-processes.
What is the first step of urine formation called?
The first step of urine formation is called pressure filtration.
What is the second step of urine formation called?
The second step of urine formation is reabsorption.
The three steps of urine formation are pressure filtration, reabsorption and which third step?
The three steps of urine formation are pressure filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion.
The three steps of urine formation are pressure filtration, tubular secretion and which other step?
The three steps of urine formation are pressure filtration, tubular secretion and reabsorption.
Which vessel carries blood to the kidney?
A renal artery carries blood to the kidney.
Into what does the renal artery divide?
The renal artery divides into many arterioles.
Each arteriole divides further into which vessels of the glomerulus?
Each arteriole divides further into the capillaries of the glomerulus.
When blood reaches the glomerulus, how is its pressure?
When blood reaches the glomerulus, its pressure is very high.
Due to the high pressure of blood in the glomerulus, materials are filtered into which structure?
Due to the high pressure of blood in the glomerulus, materials are filtered into the Bowman's capsule.
Why are blood cells and plasma proteins not filtered out of the glomerulus? They are ____ in size. Which word fills the blank?
Blood cells and plasma proteins are not filtered out of the glomerulus because they are larger in size.
In which structure does pressure filtration take place?
Pressure filtration takes place in the glomerulus.
Which of the following is NOT filtered out of the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule?
Water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes are filtered; blood cells and plasma proteins are too large.
Why are blood cells not filtered into the Bowman's capsule?
They are destroyed by the liver
Blood cells and plasma proteins are not filtered out because they are larger in size.
Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large to be filtered, so where do they stay?
Blood cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood because they are too large to be filtered.
Which statement about glomerular filtrate is correct?
It is formed after tubular secretion
It still contains useful substances such as glucose
It contains blood cells and plasma proteins
It is the same as urine
The glomerular filtrate becomes urine only after reabsorption and tubular secretion in the renal tubule.
The renal tubule is surrounded by what?
The renal tubule is surrounded by blood capillaries.
In reabsorption, the useful constituents of the glomerular filtrate go back into which vessels?
In reabsorption, the useful constituents of the glomerular filtrate go back into the blood capillaries.
Most of the water is reabsorbed from the distal convoluted tubule and which other part?
Most of the water is reabsorbed from the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct.
Some water and most of which sugar is reabsorbed from the proximal convoluted tubule?
Some water and most of the glucose is reabsorbed from the proximal convoluted tubule.
In which part of the renal tubule is most of the glucose reabsorbed?
Most of the glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Most of the water is reabsorbed in the collecting duct and which part of the renal tubule?
Most of the water is reabsorbed in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct.
Which statement about reabsorption is correct?
Useful substances move from the renal tubule back into the blood capillaries
Blood is filtered into the Bowman's capsule
Urine moves from the bladder to the urethra
Wastes move from the blood capillaries into the renal tubule
In reabsorption, the useful constituents of the glomerular filtrate go back into the blood capillaries.
Salts, hydrogen ions and which nitrogenous waste are added in tubular secretion?
Salts, hydrogen ions and urea are examples of wastes added to the renal tubule in tubular secretion.
The addition of waste materials from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule is called what?
The addition of waste materials from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule is called tubular secretion.
Which statement about tubular secretion is correct?
Wastes such as hydrogen ions and urea are added from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule
Blood cells are filtered into the Bowman's capsule
Urine is stored in the bladder
Useful substances are taken from the tubule back into the blood
In tubular secretion, waste materials are again added from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule.
After the three steps, what is the filtrate present in the renal tubule called?
After pressure filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion, the filtrate present in the renal tubule is called urine.
When the urinary bladder is filled, urine is passed out through which tube?
When the urinary bladder is filled, urine is passed out through the urethra.
From the renal pelvis, urine moves to the urinary bladder through which tubes?
From the renal pelvis, urine moves to the urinary bladder via the ureters.
A ring of which muscles near the junction of the urethra and urinary bladder controls the urine in the bladder?
A ring of sphincter muscles near the junction of the urethra and the urinary bladder controls the urine in the bladder.
Because their sphincter is not developed properly, babies cannot control what?
Because their sphincter is not developed properly, babies cannot control their urination.
Why are babies not able to control their urination?
Their kidneys do not produce urine
The sphincter muscles of the urinary bladder are not developed properly
In babies the sphincter muscles near the junction of the urethra and bladder are not developed properly.
About how much urine collected in the bladder (in ml) makes us need to discharge it?
We need to discharge urine when about 300 to 400 ml is collected in the urinary bladder.
The kidneys mainly perform osmoregulatory and which other functions?
The kidneys mainly perform osmoregulatory and excretory functions.
When water is limited in the body, what happens to the net volume of urine?
When water is limited in the body, the net volume of urine decreases.
When there is an excess of water in the body fluids, what happens to the reabsorption of water?
When there is an excess of water in the body fluids, the reabsorption of water from the filtrate is reduced.
When there is an excess of water in the body, how much urine is produced?
When there is an excess of water in the body, more urine is produced.
Human kidneys start functioning right after which month of gestation?
Human kidneys start functioning right after the fourth month of gestation.
When the amount of water in the body is limited, what happens to water?
When the amount of water in the body is limited, water is conserved in the body.
The kidneys play the most important function in which process of the body?
The kidneys play the most important function in the homeostasis of the body.
About what percentage of the glomerular filtrate does the kidney reabsorb to conserve water?
The kidney reabsorbs about 99.5% of the glomerular filtrate to conserve water.
A person drinks very little water. What happens to the reabsorption of water in the kidneys and to the volume of urine?
Less water is reabsorbed and more urine is produced
More water is reabsorbed and less urine is produced
Less water is reabsorbed and less urine is produced
More water is reabsorbed and more urine is produced
When water is limited, more water is reabsorbed from the filtrate, so the volume of urine decreases and water is conserved.
A person drinks a large amount of water. What happens in the kidneys?
Reabsorption of water increases and less urine is produced
Reabsorption of water is reduced and less urine is produced
Reabsorption of water increases and more urine is produced
Reabsorption of water is reduced and more urine is produced
With excess water, less water is reabsorbed, more water stays in the renal tubule and more urine is produced.
The situations in which the normal working of the kidneys is disturbed are called what?
The situations in which the normal working of the kidneys is disturbed are called disorders of the kidney.
High sugar in the blood damages which structures in the kidneys that function as filters?
High sugar in the blood damages the blood vessels in the kidneys that function as filters.
Damaged kidney filters in diabetes can cause weight gain and what at the ankles?
Damaged kidney filters in diabetes can cause weight gain and ankle swelling.
How does diabetes damage the kidneys?
High blood sugar damages the blood vessels that function as filters
It stops the urinary bladder from storing urine
It blocks the ureter with stones
High sugar in the blood damages the blood vessels in the kidneys, so the blood cannot be cleaned properly.
In kidney damage due to diabetes, the urine may have more of which substances?
In kidney damage due to diabetes, the urine may have more proteins.
Kidney stones are objects that cannot pass in what?
Kidney stones are objects that cannot pass in the urine.
Calcium ____ is one of the substances from which kidney stones are formed. Which word fills the blank?
Calcium oxalate is one of the substances from which kidney stones are formed.
Kidney stones are formed from calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphate and which other substance?
Kidney stones are formed from calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphate and uric acid.
Stones trapped in the ureter or urinary bladder can cause what in the urinary tract?
Stones trapped in the ureter or urinary bladder can cause obstruction in the urinary tract.
Some stones leave the kidneys and get trapped in the ureter or in which other organ?
Some stones leave the kidneys and get trapped in the ureter or the urinary bladder.
Which kind of water intake is one of the causes of kidney stones?
Reduced water intake is one of the causes of kidney stones.
Green vegetables, fats and which other food group are diet sources of stone-forming substances?
Green vegetables, fats and dairy products are the diet sources of the stone-forming substances.
Excess of which substance in the blood is one of the causes of kidney stones?
Excess uric acid in the blood is one of the causes of kidney stones.
Which type of stones are 70% of all the kidney stones?
Calcium oxalate type stones are 70% of all the kidney stones.
Which substances are present in green leafy vegetables and tomatoes?
Oxalates are present in green leafy vegetables and tomatoes.
Eating green leafy vegetables and which other food may form oxalate stones?
Eating green leafy vegetables and tomatoes may form oxalate stones.
Which of the following is NOT given as a cause of kidney stones?
Drinking plenty of water helps small stones pass; reduced water intake is one of the causes.
Extra amounts of vitamin C and which other vitamin in a diet may also cause kidney stones?
Extra amounts of vitamins C and D in a diet may also cause kidney stones.
What percentage of all kidney stones are calcium oxalate type stones?
Calcium oxalate type stones are 70% of all the kidney stones.
Patients of kidney stones feel severe what in the kidney or lower abdomen?
Patients of kidney stones feel severe pain in the kidney or lower abdomen.
A symptom of kidney stones is burning in which tube?
A symptom of kidney stones is burning in the urethra.
Foul-smelling urine, blood and pus in the urine and which other abdominal condition are symptoms of kidney stones?
Foul-smelling urine, blood and pus in the urine and bloating are symptoms of kidney stones.
Which symptom is given for kidney failure but NOT for kidney stones?
Swelling in the legs, feet and face
Severe pain in the lower abdomen
Swelling in the legs, feet and face is a symptom of kidney failure; the other options are symptoms of kidney stones.
Which symptom is given for kidney stones but NOT for kidney failure?
Swelling in the legs, feet and face
Burning in the urethra is a symptom of kidney stones, whereas weight loss and swelling are symptoms of kidney failure.
If kidney stones are small, the patient is advised to drink plenty of what?
If kidney stones are small, the patient is advised to drink plenty of water so that the stones can pass through the urine.
Fig. 11.13 shows the removal of kidney stones by which method?
Fig. 11.13 shows the removal of kidney stones by lithotripsy.
How are small kidney stones treated?
By drinking plenty of water so that they pass in the urine
If kidney stones are small, the patient is advised to drink plenty of water.
If kidney stones are large and cannot pass easily, what does the patient have to undergo?
If kidney stones are large and cannot pass easily, the patient has to undergo surgery.
In lithotripsy, the stone inside the kidney is targeted by what?
In lithotripsy, the stone inside the kidney is targeted by shock-waves.
In lithotripsy, the tiny pieces of stone are passed out of the body in what?
In lithotripsy, shock waves break the stone into tiny pieces, which are passed out of the body in the urine.
In surgery for large kidney stones, the kidney, ureter or urinary bladder is ____ and the stones are removed. Which word fills the blank?
In surgery for large kidney stones, the patient's kidney, ureter or urinary bladder is opened and the stones are removed.
Which method of removing kidney stones is non-surgical?
Lithotripsy is the non-surgical removal of kidney stones by shock-waves.
Lithotripsy works best with stones between 4 mm and what diameter?
Lithotripsy works best with stones between 4 mm and 2 cm in diameter.
Lithotripsy works best with stones that are still located in which organ?
Lithotripsy works best with stones that are still located in the kidney.
Lithotripsy can also break up stones in the ureter, but with what degree of success?
Lithotripsy can also break up stones in the ureter, but with less success.
In renal failure, which structures are progressively destroyed and stop functioning?
In renal failure, the nephrons are progressively destroyed and stop functioning.
Kidney failure is also called which failure?
Kidney failure is also called renal failure.
The two types of treatment for renal failure are dialysis and which other?
The two types of treatment for renal failure are dialysis and kidney transplantation.
In renal failure, the level of which nitrogenous waste in the blood increases?
In renal failure, the level of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood increases.
The most common causes of kidney failure are long-term diabetes mellitus and which other condition?
The most common causes of kidney failure are long-term diabetes mellitus and hypertension.
Long-term hypertension and which other disease are the most common causes of kidney failure?
Long-term diabetes mellitus and hypertension are the most common causes of kidney failure.
Swelling in the legs, feet and face in kidney failure is due to excess what in the body?
Swelling in the legs, feet and face in kidney failure is due to excess fluid in the body.
In renal failure, what are the nephrons not able to do properly to the blood?
In renal failure, the nephrons are not able to filter the blood properly.
Which of the following is NOT a cause of kidney failure mentioned in the chapter?
Drinking eight glasses of water daily
Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, severe infections and overuse of some medicines can cause kidney failure.
Overuse of aspirin, ibuprofen, cocaine and which other medicine can cause kidney failure?
Overuse of medicines such as aspirin, ibuprofen, cocaine and acetaminophen can cause kidney failure.
What is the cleaning of the blood of a patient suffering from renal failure by artificial methods called?
The cleaning of the blood of a patient suffering from renal failure by artificial methods is called dialysis.
How many methods of dialysis are there?
There are two methods of dialysis.
In dialysis, the blood and a dialysis fluid are kept on opposite sides of what?
In dialysis, the blood and a dialysis fluid are kept on opposite sides of a membrane.
In dialysis, where do the nitrogenous wastes of the blood go after passing through the membrane?
In dialysis, the nitrogenous wastes of the blood pass through the membrane and enter the dialysis fluid.
In haemodialysis, the blood is passed through which machine?
In haemodialysis, the blood is passed through a machine called a dialyzer.
The dialyzer contains tubes whose walls are made of what kind of membranes?
The dialyzer contains tubes whose walls are made of semi-permeable membranes.
In the dialyzer, where does the blood flow in relation to the tubes?
In the dialyzer, the blood flows inside the tubes.
In haemodialysis, how do extra water and wastes pass from the blood into the dialysis fluid?
In haemodialysis, extra water and wastes diffuse from the blood into the dialysis fluid.
In haemodialysis, the purified blood is returned back to where?
In haemodialysis, the purified blood is returned back to the body.
Which statement about haemodialysis is correct?
Blood flows outside the tubes while the dialysis fluid flows inside
Blood flows inside the semi-permeable tubes of the dialyzer while the dialysis fluid flows outside
Dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through a catheter
A healthy kidney of a donor is matched with the immune system
In haemodialysis, blood flows inside the tubes of the dialyzer and the dialysis fluid flows outside.
Which form of dialysis can be done at home?
Peritoneal dialysis can be done at home.
The space around the gut in the abdomen is called which cavity?
In the abdomen, the space around the gut (alimentary canal) is called the peritoneal cavity.
The walls of the peritoneal cavity are lined by a thin membrane called what?
The walls of the peritoneal cavity are lined by a thin membrane called the peritoneum.
The peritoneum has a large number of what in it?
The peritoneum has a large number of blood vessels in it.
In peritoneal dialysis, the dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through what?
In peritoneal dialysis, the dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through a catheter.
In peritoneal dialysis, how do wastes in the blood vessels of the peritoneal membrane pass into the dialysis fluid?
In peritoneal dialysis, wastes in the blood vessels of the peritoneal membrane diffuse into the dialysis fluid.
In peritoneal dialysis, what is done with the dialysis fluid after some time?
In peritoneal dialysis, after some time the dialysis fluid is drained.
Which statement about peritoneal dialysis is correct?
Blood is passed through a dialyzer outside the body
